item.title: Tea Label's Origins Reevaluated as 19th-Century Artifact
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Original headline: Here’s the tea
Tristan Brown, an MIT history professor, reevaluated a Chinese tea chest label claimed to be from the 1773 Boston Tea Party. After research, he concluded the label was created nearly a century later. The key evidence was deciphering the Chinese text as Cantonese phonetics, revealing it belonged to Smith, Archer & Co., a 19th-century US firm trading Asian tea. Collaborating with the Wells family, Brown traced the label to a relative who operated a California Tea Store during the Gold Rush. He argues the label's revolutionary claims likely emerged during 1870s centennial commemorations. The discovery highlights how objects gain historical authority and how memory shapes history. 'History is never finished,' Brown said, noting even museum artifacts can reveal new stories with fresh questions. The label's true origin challenges its status as a Boston Tea Party artifact but underscores broader themes of historical interpretation.

item.title: OpenAI Launches 'Locked Chats' for ChatGPT Privacy
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch, Engadget, PCMag Original headline: OpenAI Introduces 'Locked Chats' Feature for Enhanced Privacy in ChatGPT
OpenAI has added a 'Locked Chats' feature to ChatGPT, enabling users to secure sensitive conversations with a four-digit PIN, facial recognition, or fingerprint scan. The tool is intended for scenarios where users share devices, such as in public settings or with others. Locked chats are stored separately from regular history, with hidden titles requiring authentication to access. The feature is being rolled out gradually to most account types except ChatGPT for Healthcare. Resetting the PIN permanently deletes all locked content, including files and protected data. OpenAI notes that locked chats do not provide end-to-end encryption and do not alter data handling or legal obligations. Certain chat types, like temporary or group conversations, cannot be locked. Voice mode is available for locked chats on Android and iOS, though Codex conversations remain ineligible. The 'Improve the model for everyone' setting still applies to locked chats unless users opt out.

item.title: Danfoss Supermarket Systems Vulnerable to Remote Takeover
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Original headline: A nightmare scenario for supermarkets: Hidden daily passwords and command injection flaws leave thousands of Danfoss supermarket systems open to remote takeover
Security researchers identified three critical vulnerabilities in Danfoss refrigeration controllers used in supermarkets and warehouses. Claroty’s Team82 discovered 2,765 publicly accessible systems through internet scanning. CVE-2025-41450 allows attackers to bypass administrator passwords using a daily generated code, reconstructed from firmware analysis. CVE-2025-41451 enables command injection via email configuration, risking remote code execution. CVE-2025-41452 lets attackers modify Nginx server settings, potentially causing denial of service by disrupting web management functions. The flaws could grant unauthorized access to refrigeration systems, risking both data exposure and operational disruptions. Danfoss released firmware R4.3.1 to address the issues, urging users to update and secure administrative interfaces to trusted networks.

item.title: New Jersey Online Casinos Outearn Atlantic City in September 2026
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Original headline: New Jersey online casinos win $274.8 million in September, outearning Atlantic City floors
New Jersey online casinos generated $274.8 million in September 2026, the third-highest monthly win in state history, surpassing Atlantic City’s casino floors. Online revenue rose 12.0% from July’s $276.9 million but lagged behind August’s $259.3 million. Atlantic City’s casinos, which took $294.9 million in August, saw a 5.5% decline in September. Analyst Brian Tyrrell noted land-based casinos faced their worst September in recent history after a strong summer. Online growth remained steady despite a 15% to 19.75% tax rate increase in July 2025, with the state collecting $82.7 million in gaming taxes for September. Total 2026 gaming revenue hit $5.39 billion, up 5.1% from 2025. BetFanatics’ online win surged 187% to $14.7 million. Sports betting declined due to fewer football weekends and competition from prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket. Virginia’s online casino bills failed to pass in 2026, requiring a new attempt in 2027.

item.title: Eight Compromised TLS Certificates Spark Global Security Alert
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Original headline: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs
Eight TLS certificates from India-based certificate authority eMudhra Limited were found to have private keys so weak they could enable unauthorized trusted credentials for any website. Browser makers and major apps blocked the certificates after discovering the vulnerability. A digitally signed advisory on emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com warned of the issue, with the message 'We have a problem here – Wayne.' Cryptography engineer Filippo Valsorda called the cleanup effort 'bigger than Heartbleed,' citing challenges in updating Linux distributions, IoT devices, Docker containers, and unmaintained CLI tools. The threat remains significant as many systems may still rely on outdated root certificates, leaving millions of servers vulnerable to forged credentials. Updates are ongoing, but system administrators face a prolonged process to secure all affected devices.

item.title: Anthropic’s cloud partnerships are getting messy
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
Anthropic is struggling to secure sufficient cloud capacity from AWS, Google, and Microsoft, which now view the Claude maker as a competitor rather than a customer, according to a leaked S-1 filing. The filing reveals Anthropic could spend over $750 billion on cloud contracts, some still in negotiation, but remains concerned about third-party data center operators' reliability. The company reported an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of the year, despite $16.3 billion in revenue, with two customers accounting for about 20% of sales. It also warns of potential liability for AI-related damages exceeding insurance coverage. Recent filings show third-quarter revenue reached $16.8 billion, up 45% from the prior quarter, with an IPO planned for November. Anthropic did not comment on the reports.

item.title: Spotify Removes 50M AI-Generated Tracks This Year
item.description:
Source: Engadget, Gizmodo Original headline: Spotify Combats AI-Generated 'Slop and Spam' with Major Content Removals
Spotify removed over 50 million tracks labeled as 'slop and spam' this year, according to a blog post. The company previously deleted more than 75 million spammy tracks in 2025 due to repeated rule violations. AI-generated audio has become a growing challenge, with Spotify analyzing user behavior to identify tracks skipped, ignored, or reported by listeners. The company updated its recommendation system to prioritize music from human artists and exclude AI-generated content from curated playlists. This change reduced listener complaints about AI tracks. However, spammers continue evolving tactics to evade detection, requiring ongoing system updates. Spotify uses metadata, user feedback, upload patterns, and third-party AI detection tools to identify problematic content. Despite efforts, some AI artists, like Sienna Rose and The Velvet Sundown, have gained hundreds of thousands of monthly listeners, with one topping a Billboard chart. The top 10 AI artists on Spotify generated about $2.4 million in revenue, raising concerns about unfair competition. Spotify also implemented a 1,000-stream annual threshold for royalty eligibility and verified artist accounts for over 99% of search traffic. Meanwhile, AI music tools like Suno face lawsuits over copyright issues and have introduced watermarking and download limits to combat misuse.

item.title: U.S. Army Tests AI Agents for Offense in Cyber Warfare
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: U.S. Army developing program that would deploy AI agents to autonomously seek and destroy targets in enemy digital infrastructures
The U.S. Army is developing a program called ECHOTRIBBLE to deploy autonomous AI agents capable of seeking and destroying targets in enemy digital infrastructures. According to leaked documents from the Army Cyber Command, the agents would function like computer worms, stealthily navigating adversary networks, self-replicating across systems, and neutralizing threats by disabling or deleting them before self-destructing. Cybersecurity experts warn of risks, citing incidents where AI agents have executed unplanned tasks. They question whether self-replicating offensive agents could bypass safeguards or cause unintended damage. Hyrum Anderson of Abundant Security noted concerns about AI making unpredictable decisions, while William Marcellino of RAND highlighted the lack of human judgment in current AI systems. The program, in its early prototyping phase, is led by ARCYBER, ArCTIC, and CFIC, with private vendors submitting proposals. A virtual assessment event evaluated 65 whitepapers, narrowing them to five finalists for funding and contracts.

item.title: Chrome Adds Warnings for Suspicious Websites
item.description:
Source: The Verge - Cybersecurities Original headline: Chrome will now show a warning before you visit ‘suspicious’ sites
Google is introducing a new Chrome browser feature that warns users before visiting websites deemed 'suspicious' when Enhanced Protection mode is enabled. The system uses a two-stage warning approach, similar to its 2024 file download alerts. Suspicious sites receive a 'lower confidence verdict' indicating potential risk but not certain harm, with a pop-up warning that darkens the webpage and allows users to mark the site as safe if flagged incorrectly. Dangerous sites trigger a more intrusive warning with a full-screen red background and higher risk assessment. The update also enhances Gemini-powered scam detection for Enhanced Protection users. The warnings aim to help users distinguish between risky and harmful URLs, with the suspicious alerts providing a less disruptive experience compared to the more severe dangerous site notifications.

item.title: Modal uses Nvidia's Vera CPUs in tests showing 2x throughput over Intel and AMD
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Modal taps Nvidia Vera CPUs after firm's internal tests show 2x throughput over Intel and AMD chips
Nvidia's Vera CPUs have been selected by AI cloud provider Modal after internal tests showed twice the throughput compared to current AMD and Intel processors. Modal's evaluation indicates Vera could enhance performance for agentic AI workloads, which require substantial CPU resources for autonomous operations. The company plans to continue using x86 CPUs from AMD and Intel while adopting Vera for specific tasks, operating a heterogeneous server fleet. Nvidia expects Vera sales to reach $20 billion this fiscal year, with a potential $200 billion market. The decision follows Modal's $750 million funding round, which valued the company at $15.75 billion. Modal's CEO, Erik Bernhardsson, noted the need for software modifications to support Arm ISA, though the company will evaluate future AMD and Intel processors. Tests compared Vera against existing AMD and Intel chips, not upcoming generations. Modal's service consumption has grown 3X in 12 months, with revenue surging over 15 times year-over-year.

item.title: Apple Watch Doesn't Need Frequent Reboots, But Restarting Can Help in Some Cases
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: How often should you restart your Apple Watch?
Apple Watch doesn't require frequent restarts, but reboots can resolve issues. WatchOS is designed to manage background processes and caches, reducing the need for manual intervention. Apple recommends restarting only if experiencing bugs, freezes, or unresponsiveness. Force restart by holding side button and Digital Crown until Apple logo appears. For routine maintenance, focus on app and OS updates, and manage storage to prevent cache bloat. Manual cache clearing is possible via Settings > General > Website Data. Preventative reboots aren't necessary for most users, as watchOS handles system upkeep. Restarting during software updates ensures smooth operation, but daily use typically doesn't require it. Users can go years without manual restarts without performance issues.

item.title: Polestar studies driver experience with Oxford research on electric performance cars
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Original headline: Polestar tries to quantify what it’s like to drive a performance car
Polestar partnered with the University of Oxford to study how driving performance affects the human experience. The research focuses on electric vehicles, which redefine performance metrics beyond traditional speed and acceleration. Christian Samson, Polestar’s head of product attributes, explained the goal: 'Understanding the human experience behind the wheel' through engineering and driver interaction. The pilot study involved 12 drivers testing rear- and all-wheel-drive versions of the Polestar 4 at a Swedish track. Drivers wore heart rate monitors, electrodes, and gaze-tracking systems while lapping the Gotland Ring circuit. Data from telemetry, physiological responses, and post-drive interviews aimed to connect vehicle engineering with driver perception. The Polestar 4, a midsize crossover competing with the Porsche Macan, is unavailable in the U.S. The study seeks to quantify performance’s impact on the driver beyond measurable specs.

item.title: OpenAI acquires Orchestra Bio to expand biotech operations
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: OpenAI acquires startup Orchestra Bio⁠ to beef up its biotech business
OpenAI acquired Orchestra Bio, a four-year-old AI biotech startup, to enhance its life sciences research tools. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, though Orchestra had raised approximately $20 million by 2025 from investors including Andreessen Horowitz and 8VC. Orchestra develops AI agents that streamline drug-discovery processes for biotech firms, handling tasks like financial tracking and clinical trial scheduling. OpenAI plans to integrate Orchestra’s technology into Rosalind, its AI model for life sciences, and the Rosalind Workbench platform, which assists researchers in experimental planning and data analysis. The move follows OpenAI’s recent partnerships with companies like Moderna and Novo Nordisk. The acquisition reflects a broader trend of major AI labs expanding into pharmaceuticals, with startups often being absorbed rather than competed out.

item.title: Google Expands Gemini AI to Android Auto and Vehicles
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica, How-To Geek, Latest from Android Central, Engadget Original headline: Google Expands Gemini's Personal Intelligence to Android Auto and Vehicles with Google Built-in
Google is expanding Gemini's Personal Intelligence to Android Auto, enabling drivers to access contextual data from connected apps like Gmail, Calendar, and Photos for tailored AI responses. The feature, initially a paid option in 2026, is now optional, allowing users to control which apps Gemini can access while maintaining privacy safeguards. Excluded regions include the European Economic Area, UK, Nigeria, and Switzerland due to regulatory requirements like the EU's Digital Markets Act. How-To Geek noted the regional exclusions, while Engadget highlighted improved convenience for answering questions like flight status without phone checks. Android Central emphasized continuity in conversations and route generation based on past interactions. The rollout begins today, with broader availability for vehicles with Google built-in expected soon. Google aims to enhance safety and convenience by reducing driver distractions through AI-driven personalization.

item.title: Infrared Remotes Outperform Modern Protocols in Key Ways
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Original headline: This 50-year old remote control technology still does what other smart home protocols can’t
Infrared remotes, developed in the 1980s, still offer advantages over modern smart home protocols. They communicate directly via infrared pulses without requiring Wi-Fi, hubs, or network infrastructure. Unlike Zigbee, Z-Wave, Thread, or Matter, which depend on mesh networks or controllers, IR devices function with a clear line of sight between the remote and receiver. This allows control of non-smart appliances like old stereos and projectors that lack modern connectivity. Home Assistant now supports infrared natively, enabling integration of IR devices without custom scripts. IR blasters can replicate remote signals, turning non-smart devices into controllable elements. However, IR has limitations: it requires line of sight, lacks two-way communication, and can lose signals if obstructed. Despite these drawbacks, IR remains cost-effective for controlling legacy devices. Modern protocols offer features IR cannot match, but infrared still serves specific use cases in smart homes.

item.title: Hackers exploit Plex servers to mine cryptocurrency
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Original headline: Hackers are hijacking Plex servers to mine crypto. Update ASAP
Hackers are exploiting four vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server to mine cryptocurrency and route internet traffic through infected machines. Security researchers identified the flaws, collectively named Plex2Shell, which allow remote code execution without login. Attackers use the exploits to install crypto-mining software and proxy services, causing high CPU usage and performance degradation. Plex patched the vulnerabilities in September, but many users remain unpatched, leaving servers vulnerable. The company confirms widespread attacks targeting internet-accessible devices. Users are urged to check their Plex version, update to 1.43.3 or later, and run antivirus scans. A clean reinstallation is recommended if malware is detected. The vulnerabilities enable attackers to compromise servers without prior access.

item.title: MIT and EPFL Develop Robot That Flies and Swims Like Birds
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Original headline: It’s a bird, it’s a plane … it’s a robo-puffin?
Engineers at MIT and EPFL developed a robot capable of transitioning between swimming and flying, inspired by birds like puffins. The FAAV robot weighs less than 300 grams and uses flexible wings, a waterproof motor, and a motorized tail to navigate both mediums. Experiments in water tanks and Lake Geneva identified optimal wing size, flapping frequency, and tail angle for smooth transitions. Medium-sized, flexible wings minimized flapping in water while maintaining lift in air, with a 70-degree pitch enabling the leap from water to flight. The robot does not require feet for takeoff. Researchers aim to enhance the design for turbulence resistance and deploy it for ocean data collection. 'It would dive into the water to take a measurement or collect a sample, and fly back to deliver the data at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods,' says Raphael Zufferey. Future goals include testing in choppy waters and wind, enabling frequent, location-based data gathering for marine science.

item.title: Ryobi's Battery Design Keeps Old Tools Compatible with New Lithium-Ion Packs
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Original headline: Ryobi's batteries are smarter than other tool brands, but it might not be as important as it seems
Ryobi's ONE+ battery system places battery-management logic inside the pack instead of the tool, unlike competitors like Milwaukee, DeWalt, and Makita. This design allows older tools to work with modern lithium-ion batteries without requiring tool-side electronics. Ryobi's system monitors cell voltages, temperature, and current to prevent damage, cutting power via solid-state switches if thresholds are exceeded. The approach ensures compatibility across three decades of ONE+ tools, but increases battery cost and heat generation compared to rival designs that use tool-side or shared management systems. While the BMS prevents cell damage, it doesn't enhance motor performance or runtime. Other brands opted for slide-style batteries with tool-side control to reduce costs and improve heat dissipation. Ryobi's design remains practical for existing users but doesn't offer performance advantages over competing systems.

item.title: Steam Deck LCD Lifespan and Parts Availability
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: How long can you expect your original Steam Deck to last?
The original Steam Deck LCD's lifespan depends on hardware wear and part availability. Valve has not restocked OEM batteries, but iFixit sources aftermarket replacements. Battery replacement is difficult due to adhesive bonding, with DIY repairs requiring multiple videos. Valve's support team can assess repair costs, though prices for parts like batteries have risen. The device's software remains supported, running the same OS as the newer OLED model. While the Steam Deck struggles with modern AAA games, developers continue optimizing for the platform. Indie titles, retro games, and emulation provide long-term playability. Hardware failures like thumbstick drift are easier to fix, with replacement parts available. However, newer models and RAM shortages have increased costs. The original Deck may last years for older games but faces limitations with new releases. Valve's ecosystem incentives suggest ongoing support, but hardware obsolescence remains a concern.

item.title: OpenBSD 8.0 release maintains security record with new features
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Original headline: OpenBSD 8.0 arrives with security record still intact
OpenBSD 8.0 is now available, marking the project’s 61st release and continuing its semiannual schedule since 1996. Founder Theo de Raadt notes the operating system maintains a security record of over 30 years with only two remote vulnerabilities in its default install. Key updates include Intel Arc A-Series graphics support, expanded 512GB kernel virtual address space for AMD64, ARM64 hibernation, a new RPKI-to-router daemon, RISC-V vector extension support, wireless driver improvements, and virtual machine capabilities for 64 CPUs. LibreSSL 4.4.0 and OpenSSH 10.6 receive security upgrades. The release also ends support for Loongson architecture due to compatibility issues with Clang 22. Changes are detailed in the release announcement.

item.title: Google and Amazon Release PyTorch Alternatives to Challenge Nvidia
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: Google has joined Amazon in attacking Nvidia’s stronghold with AI app developers
Google and Amazon released PyTorch alternatives to reduce Nvidia's influence in AI development. Google announced TorchTPU, an open-source version of PyTorch, allowing AI apps to run on its TPUs with minimal code changes. Amazon released TorchNeuron, enabling apps to use its Trainium chips and AWS without rewriting. Both companies aim to weaken Nvidia's dominance by making PyTorch more hardware-agnostic. Google collaborated with Meta, Hugging Face, and others to ensure TorchTPU integrates with popular tools. It also launched a TPU agent suite and updated LiteRT for better PyTorch compatibility. Amazon submitted code to the main PyTorch project to decouple features from Nvidia hardware. While developers may not abandon Nvidia immediately, the moves signal a shift toward diversified AI chip ecosystems.

item.title: US Lags in Medium-Lift Rocket Development as New Competitors Emerge
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Original headline: Does anyone actually want to win the medium-lift race in the United States?
The Antares rocket, developed by Orbital Sciences Corporation, debuted in 2007 as the last U.S. medium-lift vehicle. Its 100-series variant used refurbished Soviet engines, leading to a 2014 explosion on its fifth launch. Antares, with Russian engines and Ukrainian-manufactured stages, is now obsolete as four new U.S.-built medium-lift rockets prepare to launch. These next-gen vehicles, inspired by SpaceX’s Falcon 9, prioritize in-house engine production to control costs and timelines. SpaceX plans to exit the commercial market by 2028, intensifying competition. Satellite operators face uncertainty about launch options between 2027-2030 due to unclear availability of new rockets. The Vulcan and New Glenn rockets, while capable, have high costs and limited capacity for smaller satellites. No consensus exists on which new medium-lift vehicles will scale launch frequency, creating a critical gap in commercial space capacity.

item.title: PHP to release two emergency patches for severe vulnerabilities
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Original headline: PHP warns it plans to release 2 emergency patches imminently
PHP maintainers announced plans to release two emergency patches for severe vulnerabilities rated 9.2 out of 10. The fixes, expected within 12 hours, may be released earlier if exploit details emerge or active attacks are confirmed. An unconfirmed report showed an exploit tool, PHP2Shell, targeting multiple PHP-based platforms including WordPress, MediaWiki, phpBB, Magento, Joomla, Laravel, Symphony, Drupal, and WHMCS. Security firm watchTowr claimed the vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, affect all PHP versions from 5.0 onward. The advisory urged immediate preparation for upgrades to mitigate risks. Attempts to verify the report were unsuccessful, but watchTowr confirmed the vulnerabilities' validity. PHP users are advised to monitor for updates and apply patches promptly to prevent potential breaches.

item.title: Eka Robotics Valued at $1.45B for Breakthrough Physical AI Model
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: Eka is worth $1.45B thanks to a physical AI model that has experts raving
Eka Robotics, founded by MIT professor Pulkit Agrawal and former Google DeepMind researcher Tuomas Haarnoja, closed a $150 million Series A round, valuing the company at $1.45 billion. The startup’s breakthrough lies in a physical AI model that enables robots to manipulate objects with high precision. The model, a vision-force-action system, focuses on force and touch rather than vision-language-action approaches. Experts praise its capabilities, with Raghu Raghuram of a16z calling it "superhuman" in manipulation tasks. Kris Hauser of the University of Illinois noted the robot adapts to diverse objects without retraining, achieving 95% reliability in picking up 1,500 objects per hour. The system uses reinforcement learning and physics simulations to train robots, allowing rapid scaling of experience. Agrawal argues the model bridges the generality-performance gap in robotics, enabling tasks like picking up fragile items without breaking them. Challenges remain in real-world deployment and task generalization, though Eka aims to deploy grippers with 20 million duty cycles. The company is testing industrial applications but faces hurdles in scaling from simulation to physical environments.

item.title: Neighbors Affect Smart Home Performance; Solutions Exist
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Original headline: 4 ways your neighbors are ruining your smart home (and how to fix it permanently)
Neighbors can disrupt smart home performance through shared internet, Wi-Fi interference, accidental device triggers, and data leaks. Shared internet connections cause latency when multiple users stream or download simultaneously, leading to lag in smart devices. Smart queue management on routers, using algorithms like CAKE or FQ-CoDel, can prioritize critical traffic. Low Latency DOCSIS creates a fast lane for smart devices but requires cable internet. Wi-Fi routers interfere with Zigbee/Thread protocols by occupying 2.4GHz channels, forcing smart devices to wait. Locking Wi-Fi to 20MHz channels and moving Zigbee coordinators to less overlapping channels helps. Old 315MHz/433MHz remotes can accidentally trigger devices, while new Matter/Bluetooth devices risk pairing with neighbors. Phones broadcast probe requests, allowing neighbors to track movement and routines via signal analysis. Fixes involve router settings, channel adjustments, and avoiding vulnerable frequencies, though some issues persist without hardware upgrades.

item.title: Users Use AI to Remove Ads and Trackers from Smart TVs
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Original headline: People are using AI vibe coding to remove ads and trackers from smart TVs
Developers are using AI tools to remove ads, trackers, and bloatware from smart TVs. Projects like dumbtv and cleanyourtv offer solutions via GitHub, stripping unwanted features such as ads, telemetry, and pre-installed apps. Dumbtv emphasizes a clean interface with no ads or updates, while cleanyourtv replaces the Android TV home screen with a minimalist launcher. Ryan Doyle used Claude Code on X to automate the process, eliminating bloatware and improving performance. Cretezy’s ad-free Android TV setup replaces core OS elements with custom tools, including a YouTube substitute and media manager, all configured via AI. These methods are reversible and avoid modifying the TV’s root directory. Consumer frustration with slow, ad-filled smart TVs and rising streaming costs has driven demand for such solutions. AI’s role in rapidly deploying targeted fixes has led to a surge in DIY hacks, offering users control over their devices. The trend reflects broader dissatisfaction with Big Tech’s data practices and streaming service overhauls.

item.title: Oura Ring Adds Cardiovascular Health Tracking Features
item.description:
Source: The Verge, Engadget Original headline: Oura Ring Introduces New Cardiovascular Health Tracking Features
Oura Ring Gen 3 and later models now include Cardio Effort and automatic VO2 Max features to track cardiovascular health. Cardio Effort evaluates weekly cardiovascular strain using a five-tier rating system from 'Light' to 'Reaching,' offering recovery guidance based on Training Impulse methodology. The Verge notes the feature balances training with rest by analyzing workout intensity and duration. Automatic VO2 Max replaces the previous Cardio Capacity tool, which required a six-minute walking test. New estimates are generated passively after five GPS-enabled activities like walks or runs. VO2 Max data appears in the Oura app’s My Health Heart Hub, showing current estimates, ratings, and historical trends. Engadget highlights the elimination of manual calibration, making the metric more accessible. The updates position Oura as a competitive wearable fitness option, blending performance analysis with recovery recommendations to support fitness optimization. Both features are available only to users with active Oura memberships.

item.title: AMD Zen 6 APU with 24GB LPDDR5 memory spotted in benchmarks
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Mysterious AMD Zen 6 APU with 24GB of LPDDR5 memory appears in benchmarks
An AMD engineering sample with part number 100-000001930-12_Y surfaced in OpenBenchmarking, featuring a six-core, 12-thread Zen 6 processor paired with 24GB LPDDR5 memory running at 9,600 MT/s. The chip, tested on a GBR-FF6-SKT board, operates at 2.4 GHz and includes four 6GB SK Hynix memory modules. Its microcode revision aligns with AMD’s Family 1Ah, model DCh, suggesting it could be part of the Gainsborough family. While the integrated GPU runs at 2,400 MHz, its architecture and compute units remain unspecified. Benchmark results from GpuTest show scores of 3,871 in GiMark, 3,508 in FurMark, and 9,319 in TessMark, though tests were conducted on an engineering platform with development software. The sample’s specifications could represent a hardware upgrade for a potential next-gen Steam Deck, but AMD and Valve have not confirmed its use. The results do not reflect final performance due to power limits, cooling, and driver maturity factors. Further details are pending.

item.title: Quantum error correction goes well beyond breakeven
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica
Quantum error correction has surpassed the breakeven point, where adding more hardware qubits improves logical qubit performance. However, the gains remain modest, requiring impractical numbers of qubits to achieve error rates suitable for complex algorithms. Quantinuum reported its hardware can scale beyond breakeven, with each increase in logical qubit size boosting performance by over 10 times. Logical qubits rely on entangled hardware qubits for error detection, using syndrome data from measurements to identify errors. Error correction codes vary in geometry, affecting how many qubits are needed, logical qubit capacity, and error tolerance. While progress shows logical qubits can function beyond breakeven, practical implementation for advanced computations still demands significant qubit counts. The findings highlight advancements in error correction but underscore the ongoing challenge of achieving fault-tolerant quantum computing.

item.title: Building a mechanical keyboard costs more than buying pre-built models
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: You can build your own mechanical keyboard, but is it worth the price?
Building a mechanical keyboard costs more than buying pre-built models. Custom builds require significant time and money, with cases alone often exceeding $100. Pre-built mechanical keyboards start around $50 but can cost $100 or more. DIY kits reduce assembly time by including pre-installed components like circuit boards, but prices can still rival full custom builds. Hot-swappable keyboards offer customization without full assembly, allowing switch replacements without soldering. Custom builds let users tailor switches, keycaps, and layouts for specific preferences, though the process involves research and tool use. For those prioritizing end results over process, pre-built options may be more practical. Rare switch types not available in standard models justify custom builds for some users. DIY kits and hot-swappable designs provide entry-level customization without full assembly, balancing cost and flexibility.

item.title: 1kW Wind Turbine Provides Limited Home Power, Depends on Wind and Location
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: How much power can a 1kW wind turbine produce for your home?
A 1 kW wind turbine can produce up to 2,400 kWh annually in optimal conditions, meeting about a quarter of the average US household's energy needs. However, output depends heavily on wind speed, requiring average annual speeds of 14+ mph. Obstacles like trees, buildings, or hills reduce efficiency by blocking wind and causing turbulence. The Department of Energy recommends placing the turbine rotor at least 30 feet above nearby obstacles within 300 feet. Zoning laws often limit structures to 35 feet, making rooftop installations problematic due to noise and vibration. A 1 kW system is suitable for small homes or RVs but insufficient for typical US households, which consume around 10,500 kWh yearly. Costs range from $20,000 to $50,000 for turbines, compared to $2,500 to $3,500 for solar panels. Grid-connected systems need inverters, while off-grid setups require batteries. Wind power is most viable in rural areas with consistent wind and space for towers.

item.title: Netflix Slows Revenue Growth, Faces Investor Concerns Over Strategic Shifts
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo, The Verge Original headline: Netflix Faces Investor Concerns Over Slowing Growth and Strategic Restructuring
Netflix reported third-quarter earnings showing slower revenue growth and revised ad revenue forecasts, sparking investor concerns. The company warned of reduced revenue increases and adjusted its ad revenue projection to $2.7 billion from $3 billion. A 6% stock price decline followed the report, with analysts citing a drop in U.S. viewing hours to 49 per month per user from 66 in 2023. Netflix’s U.S. viewing share fell to 7.8% in July, down one percentage point year-over-year. The firm laid off 1,000 employees, its largest reduction in four years, and replaced key executives, including chief content officer Bela Bajaria. Co-CEO Ted Sarandos acknowledged challenges in the U.S. market, noting international regions drive growth but new hit shows are scarce domestically. Netflix plans to expand ad-supported tiers to 15 countries by 2027 and diversify content through partnerships like NFL games and TF1. Competitors like HBO Max and Paramount Plus are merging, while YouTube offers creators millions to avoid posting on Netflix. The company’s ability to revamp content strategy and regain viewer engagement remains critical to its future.

item.title: Startup Develops AI to Decipher Plant Electrical Signals
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: Plants can speak using electricity, so this startup built an AI model to decipher their language
Justin Mast and neuroscientist Lee von Kraus founded Electric Plant to develop an AI model called Bombadil that interprets electrical signals from plants. The startup spent three years collecting data to create the model, which analyzes subtle electrical changes in plant stems to relay their needs to growers. Electric Plant raised $11.2 million in seed funding to commercialize its sensors and AI system. The sensors, costing tens of dollars versus thousands for existing tools, detect microvolt changes by penetrating a plant’s cambium layer. Data is transmitted via low-power wireless networks to a cloud-based system for analysis. Mast claims the technology could boost crop yields while reducing water use by 20% or more. Bombadil currently supports 125 plant species, including ferns, redwoods, tomatoes, and dahlias. Mast emphasized the model’s diversity, calling it the most comprehensive ever created for biological electrical signals. The startup aims to provide real-time insights for agriculture and forestry, though it hasn’t disclosed initial customers.

item.title: GM Closes Detroit Battery Plant Due to Lease Expiry
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: GM to close Detroit battery-assembly plant, but not for reasons you might think
GM is closing the Brownstown Battery Assembly Plant south of Detroit, a spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch. The facility produced battery packs for Cadillac’s Celestiq and Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray, as well as electric drive units. The closure stems from the lease ending, not GM’s electric vehicle strategy. Employees and operations will be relocated to other GM facilities, though specific locations were not disclosed. The decision follows the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s repeal of EV production and sales incentives, which disrupted automakers’ electrification plans. Despite reduced public commentary on EVs, GM continues producing EVs like the Chevrolet Silverado EV and Bolt. The company also researches new battery chemistries, including lithium-manganese-rich and sodium-ion, and is expanding a $900 million facility to accelerate battery commercialization.

item.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 Action Button Offers Multiple Customizable Functions
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: What can you use your Apple Watch Ultra 4 action button for?
The Apple Watch Ultra 4's action button offers multiple customizable functions for users. It can start workouts, activate emergency sirens, control flashlights, record voice memos, and manage navigation tools like waypoints and backtrack. Users can assign one primary function at a time, with options to switch functions quickly via the Quick Switch menu. The button also supports advanced automation through Shortcuts, allowing users to trigger complex routines like adjusting smart home devices or playing local news. New features in watchOS 27 and iOS 27 simplify shortcut creation by enabling voice-based automation. The button's versatility makes it a key feature for outdoor activities and daily tasks, though it's absent on standard Apple Watch models. Apple highlights its utility for emergency situations and repetitive actions, emphasizing its role in enhancing productivity and safety.

item.title: Google Introduces Fitbit Edge as Mid-Range Fitness Tracker
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: Fitbit Edge vs. Fitbit Inspire 3: How these Google fitness trackers compare
Google has released the Fitbit Edge, a mid-range fitness tracker positioned between a basic tracker and a full smartwatch. The Edge features a larger AMOLED screen, 100% recycled aluminum case, and built-in GPS for 40% more accurate movement tracking. It also includes Bluetooth 5.4 for direct headphone connectivity and supports features like Quick Replies, music controls, and weather forecasts. The Edge can track over 50 exercise modes and offers advanced health metrics such as 24/7 heart rate, ECG with irregular heartbeat detection, and blood pressure insights. It retails for $180, compared to the $99.95 Fitbit Inspire 3, which lacks GPS, Bluetooth 5.4, and advanced health sensors. Both devices share 5 ATM water resistance but only the Edge has IP68 dust resistance. The Edge’s battery lasts up to a week, slightly shorter than the Inspire 3’s 10-day lifespan. The Edge is marketed as a premium alternative to the Pixel Watch 5, offering more fitness data without full smartwatch features.

item.title: Google Expands 3D Emoji Rollout to Older Pixel Phones
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Original headline: Google's new 3D emojis are starting to roll out to older Pixel phones
Google is rolling out its new Noto 3D emojis to older Pixel phones. The redesigned emojis, introduced with Android 17 and the Pixel 11 series, have started appearing on devices like the Pixel 6a via system updates, according to a Reddit user. While the rollout is limited, Google confirmed plans to expand the emojis to all Android phones. The new design adds depth and dimension, addressing past complaints about Android's plain emoji appearance. However, devices such as the Pixel 9a and 9 Pro running Android 17 have not yet received the update. Google also aims to bring the emojis to devices from manufacturers like Xiaomi, OnePlus, and Motorola. The gradual rollout suggests broader distribution may occur in the coming weeks.

item.title: Microsoft Fixes Windows 11 Audio Bug Causing Crashes
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Original headline: Windows 11’s audio bug that’s crashing games and apps is now fixed
Microsoft has fixed a Windows 11 audio bug that caused crashes in games and apps. The issue originated with the September release of update KB5124010, which disrupted Dolby Digital AC-3 audio decoding. This led to crashes when adjusting volume or using specific audio functions, with some apps and games failing to launch. Microsoft addressed the problem in October’s KB5127648 update, available for Windows 11 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2. Users experiencing AC-3 audio issues are advised to install the latest update via Windows Update. The fix resolves the built-in audio decoding problem, though programs using their own decoding components remained unaffected.

item.title: Gamer uses Claude AI to boost Oblivion Remastered performance by 68%
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Oblivion gamer uses Claude AI to boost average FPS gains up to 48%, stutters slashed by 90%
Gamer LTSharpe used Claude AI to significantly improve performance in The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Remastered. The mod addresses stuttering and low FPS by optimizing hardware utilization without altering visuals. LTSharpe, using a Ryzen 7 5800X and Radeon GPU, reverse-engineered the game's Unreal Engine and underlying Gamebryo code to fix bugs in AMD's frame generation and Unreal Engine itself. Performance gains reached 68% in worst-case scenarios, with average FPS increases up to 48% and stuttering reduced by 90%. Fixes were tailored to his system, addressing issues with AMD's FSR upscaling during window switching. The mod, available on NexusMods, is designed for AMD users and includes support for troubleshooting. LTSharpe encourages other gamers to test the fix and report results.

item.title: AMD's FSR 4.1 Upcoming on Xbox Consoles
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: AMD is bringing its next-gen FSR 4.1 upscaling tech to Xbox
AMD announced FSR 4.1 upscaling technology will arrive on Xbox Series X/S, Ally X, Ally X20, Ally S, and Ally handheld consoles. The tech uses machine learning to upscale lower-resolution game renders for sharper visuals while conserving resources. Performance gains are expected for Series S and older Ally models. Xbox CTO Scott Van Vilet noted AMD's collaboration to provide developers with enhanced performance and visual quality tools. Release dates remain unspecified, though a video suggests Ally X may receive the update before year-end. Other consoles are listed as 'coming soon' with no confirmed timeline. AMD also plans to expand FSR 4.1 to RX 6000-series GPUs and Ryzen AI 9 laptops. Sony's Quick Spectral Super Resolution, available on PS5 and PS5 Pro, offers similar upscaling capabilities.

item.title: Robotic System Combines AI and Therapists for Stroke Rehabilitation
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Original headline: Robotic therapy for stroke patients
Strokes leave 5 million people with long-term impairments annually, but a shortage of physical therapists limits access to care. Johannes Lachner and Noah Geiger developed a robotic system that integrates generative AI and real-time force feedback to assist stroke patients during rehabilitation. The system learns from human therapists to provide tailored support for exercises like arm lifting and daily tasks. Lachner emphasized the goal is to 'extend therapists' reach,' not replace them. Initial experiments confirmed the approach's feasibility, with plans for long-term clinical trials using the same patients who previously received manual therapy. The technology could also apply to industrial settings requiring human-robot collaboration. The project aims to address care gaps while expanding therapeutic capabilities through AI integration.

item.title: Hobbyist Transforms $120 SODIMM Kit into $1000 Desktop RAM
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Electronics hobbyist converts $120 DDR5 SODIMM kit into ‘$1000’ desktop kit to fight RAM crisis
Blighted Agent converted a $120 SK hynix DDR5-5600 SODIMM laptop kit into a desktop DDR5-7800 module worth around $1,000. The process involved purchasing DDR5 desktop PCBs for $16 each and heatsinks for $18, bringing total costs to $175. Using flux, a preheater, and hot air, the hobbyist soldered the SODIMM ICs onto blank PCBs, then added SPD and BIOS chips. The resulting modules were tested on an Asus motherboard, recognized as 5600MHz sticks, and tuned to run at 7800MHz with 1.40V. Stress testing confirmed stability for gaming. The project highlights a workaround for DDR5 RAM shortages, as new 32GB DDR5-6000 kits cost $449. Blighted Agent notes risks in BGA soldering and lack of testing tools, but claims success without issues. Similar efforts by Russian enthusiast VIK-on earlier this year used custom firmware for XMP support. DDR5 remains expensive, with used SODIMMs often costing over $300 on eBay.

item.title: Ketogenic Diet Linked to Higher Small Intestine Cancer Risk in Mice
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Original headline: A reason to eat carbs
A study led by Omer Yilmaz and colleagues found that a ketogenic diet, which forces the body to burn fat instead of carbohydrates, increases small intestine tumor risk in mice. The research showed that fatty acid oxidation in intestinal cells activates proteins that accelerate stem cell proliferation, potentially leading to tumor formation. While the diet suppressed colon tumor development, ketone bodies like BHB were not responsible for the protective effect. Yilmaz noted ketone supplements likely have minimal impact on health. The study highlights conflicting effects of the same diet on adjacent gut regions, with Chi emphasizing the need to understand why. The findings caution against generalizing diet effects, as the ketogenic approach may benefit one part of the gut while harming another.

item.title: Mods boost DLSS 5 performance with foveated rendering techniques
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Mods can almost double DLSS 5 performance through Foveation, reducing resolution at the edges of frames
Mods using foveated imaging techniques can nearly double DLSS 5 performance by reducing GPU load. ReShade, a graphics modding tool, now includes foveated rendering add-ons like Foveated DLSS5 and CheekyFoveatedDLSS. These tools adjust DLSS 5 Neural Rendering to prioritize detail in the central vision area while lowering resolution at frame edges, mimicking human eye behavior. Foveated DLSS5, a ReShade add-on, and CheekyFoveatedDLSS, a standalone integration, allow users to customize the focus area's size and render fall-off rate. Performance gains include a reported 48 to 80 FPS increase in The Witcher 3 on an RTX 4090. CheekyFoveatedDLSS is praised for being more convenient and polished, though ReShade's pipeline is longer. Both implementations make DLSS 5 more feasible for high-resolution, ultrawide displays by minimizing resource-intensive rendering outside the central field of view.

item.title: 5 ways to make your old iPhone feel faster
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Slow iPhone? Clean storage, optimize iCloud, offload apps, disable animations, and check battery health to improve performance. Running out of storage causes slowdowns by limiting cache and wear leveling. Free up space by deleting unused apps, media, and messages via Settings > General > iPhone Storage. Enable iCloud Photos optimization to offload high-resolution media. Clear Safari website data and disable Background App Refresh to reduce hardware strain. Reduce motion and transparency effects in Accessibility settings for smoother performance. Check battery health in Settings > Battery > Battery Health; replace batteries if capacity drops below 80% (costs $69–$129). A clean restore may also revive older devices by erasing all data and resetting settings. These steps can extend iPhone lifespan without upgrading.

item.title: Smart TV Platforms Compared: Apple TV, Fire TV, Google TV, Roku
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: Every Smart TV Platform Compared: Apple TV vs. Fire TV vs. Google TV vs. Roku
Smart TV platforms differ in features, app support, and voice assistant integration. Fire TV, available on Amazon TVs and streamers, prioritizes Amazon content and includes Alexa with Alexa+ for voice control. It lacks Google Cast and has limited AirPlay support on streamers. Apple TV uses tvOS, requiring a dedicated Apple TV 4K device for full features like hands-free Siri and AirPlay. It lacks standalone TVs and has no Chromecast support. Google TV combines old and new systems, supporting Chromecast and some AirPlay via manufacturer additions. It uses Google Assistant and Gemini AI, with Gemini requiring a subscription. Roku offers an intuitive interface but lacks Twitch and Chromecast support. LG's webOS supports AirPlay, Miracast, and Google Cast, integrating ThinQ for smart home control. Most platforms include major streaming apps, but Roku excludes Twitch. Voice assistants vary by platform, with Alexa, Siri, and Google Assistant offering different smart home and AI capabilities.

item.title: Windows 11 lets users close apps with two clicks
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Original headline: Frozen apps on Windows 11? Try this two-click trick
Windows 11 allows users to close unresponsive applications with two clicks. Right-clicking an app's taskbar icon and selecting 'End Task' terminates it immediately, bypassing the normal exit process. This differs from 'Close Window,' which lets the app save data before closing. File Explorer lacks the 'End Task' option, requiring Task Manager for forced closure. To enable 'End Task,' navigate to Settings > System > Advanced, toggle the switch next to 'End Task' to On. The option appears in the taskbar's context menu only when the app is running. The feature is not enabled by default.

item.title: Spotify Enforces QR Code Verification for Family Plan Members
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: Spotify Cracks Down on Family Plan Sharing With QR Code Verification
Spotify requires Family plan users to verify membership via QR code scanning. Members must complete verification within seven days of receiving a notification, or face a 12-month ban from new Family or Duo plans. The plan manager generates a QR code through their profile settings, which the member scans to confirm. Spotify notes the QR code changes every few seconds, limiting the effectiveness of screenshots. The Premium Family plan costs $21.99 monthly, allowing up to six members, compared to the $12.99 Individual plan. This is Spotify’s second measure to prevent password sharing, following address verification requirements.

item.title: Apple Limits iPhone Duo Purchases to Two Per Customer
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: Apple Limits iPhone Duo Orders to 2 Per Customer Amid Long Delivery Waits
Apple restricts iPhone Duo purchases to two per customer. The limit, set at $6,400 for two 2TB models, appears during checkout with a message stating, 'A maximum of 2 iPhone Duos can be purchased per customer.' Restrictions were less visible in the US compared to China and Hong Kong. Orders placed last Friday now face December delivery, with some shifted to late November. Estimated delivery dates on Apple's site show January arrivals, but adjustments have occurred. Scalpers have sold Duos on eBay for over $5,000. The policy's purpose remains unclear, with possibilities including combating resellers or canceled orders.

item.title: Snap hires Robert Downey Jr. to promote AR glasses
item.description:
Source: The Verge Original headline: Snap is paying Robert Downey Jr. to do the Iron Man thing
Snap has appointed Robert Downey Jr. as Chief Customer Experience Officer for its Specs AR glasses. Downey will promote the product through videos demonstrating features like helping with a golf putt, practicing art, and watching private MMA matches. He also mocked Meta’s smart glasses by discarding a box labeled 'AI glasses' into a trash bin. Downey stated he was 'absolutely sold on SPECS within 40 seconds' after testing wearable tech for 20 years. The partnership includes other celebrities like Imogen Heap and Jimmy Butler. Specs will launch this fall at $2,195, with pre-orders now available. The glasses aim to enhance daily life through augmented reality in fields like medicine and engineering.

item.title: JustWatch launches streaming service to compete with free and paid platforms
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: Streaming guide JustWatch becomes a streamer itself
JustWatch, the company behind the popular streaming guide used by 50 million people, is launching its own streaming service called JustWatch TV. The new platform will feature content from 30 partners, including Paramount, New Regency, and Fremantle, and will offer both free and paid tiers. The free tier includes ad-supported titles, while the paid tier, JustWatch TV Plus, offers over 300 ad-free titles in the U.S. and additional features like advanced filters. The service will be available in 12 markets, including the U.S., U.K., Germany, and Australia. A movie rental store will also debut in select regions. Quentin Carbonell, JustWatch’s SVP of Global Content Acquisitions and Strategy, stated the move aims to grow the company’s audience while supporting its existing partners. The service will compete with low-cost streamers like Roku’s Howdy, priced at $3.99 monthly or $49.99 annually. Content focuses on older films, indie titles, and user-requested additions. The platform’s data will also be used for targeted marketing campaigns across social media platforms.

item.title: Apple to Announce Mac and iPad Updates at October 28 Event
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: What to expect at Apple's 'Pro and Tell' event on October 28
Apple will host a product briefing on October 28 in Los Angeles, focusing on Mac and iPad updates. Key rumored announcements include a touchscreen MacBook Pro with an OLED display, thinner bezels, and a Dynamic Island design, though it will retain the M5 Pro/M5 Max chip instead of the M6. The M6 chip is expected to power other Macs, including the entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro and the iMac, offering improved performance and AI capabilities. The iPad mini is also likely to receive an OLED display upgrade, alongside the A20 Pro chip, thinner bezels, and potential water resistance. The event will not feature a traditional product launch but will serve as a press briefing for creators. Details remain speculative, with confirmed updates pending Apple's October 28 announcement.

item.title: Claude identifies three critical homelab issues overlooked by user
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Original headline: I gave Claude the keys to my homelab, and it found 3 major problems I'd overlooked for months
Claude identified three critical issues in the user's homelab. First, backups were missing key services because the user had manually excluded them, leaving new services unbacked up. Second, an ISP change altered IPv6 addresses, breaking some services that relied on the outdated IPv6 DNS setup. Third, Proxmox on one machine remained unupdated due to incorrect configuration, missing critical security patches. The user had not noticed these problems as systems functioned normally. Solutions included restoring default backup settings, enabling free Proxmox updates, and adjusting DNS configurations. The user emphasized that even if systems appear operational, hidden issues can persist, highlighting the value of AI-assisted audits for homelab maintenance.

item.title: Nebraska native studies galaxy clusters to understand universe's composition
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Original headline: Nebraska native explores galaxies far, far away
Megan Donahue, a physics and astronomy professor at Michigan State University, traces her scientific journey to a small Nebraska farm and a local library. At 12, she discovered her passion for physics through reading, leading to a pivotal experience in MIT’s Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program. There, she worked on cutting-edge x-ray imaging, which sparked her interest in astronomy. Her current research focuses on galaxy clusters and baryonic matter to understand the universe’s composition and evolution. Donahue, who served as president of the American Astronomical Society from 2018 to 2020, compares galaxy clusters to large samples of the universe, emphasizing their importance in studying cosmic structure. She describes them as 'very large scoops of the universe,' akin to sampling ocean water to determine its average composition.

item.title: Developer Creates AI-Assisted Driver for Windows 98 SE USB4 Support
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Windows 98 SE users get a Thunderbolt 4 driver, thanks to AI assistance
Developer Yeo Kheng Meng released xHCI98 v3.0.0.0, an experimental driver enabling USB4 and Thunderbolt 3/4 support on Windows 98 SE, ME, 2000, XP, Vista, and 7. The driver allows hotplugging of USB devices and supports Thunderbolt docks, NVMe enclosures, and UAS storage. Meng, a retrocomputing enthusiast, explains that older OSes lack xHCI drivers, forcing reliance on legacy BIOS support. He developed the project with AI assistance from Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, and Codex GPT 6 Astra, acknowledging potential bugs. Testing focused on Intel hardware, with a demo showing compatibility on a 2020 ThinkPad P14s Gen 1. The driver replaces Windows’ USB drivers and includes guidance for installation and tuning. Meng notes limitations, including issues with standby, hibernation, and hardware compatibility, while emphasizing the project fills a gap for users with xHCI-only chipsets lacking legacy EHCI controllers.

item.title: Ukraine uses drone to rescue wounded soldier from frontline
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Original headline: Ukraine’s drone rescue of wounded soldier puts much touted idea into practice
Ukraine used a heavy hexacopter drone to rescue a wounded soldier from a frontline position where Russian drones and landmines made ground evacuation impractical. The operation, revealed after testing drones for casualty evacuation, involved the Heavy Shot AYUDAG 6 model provided by Gurzuf Defence. The soldier, from the 30th separate mechanized brigade, had spent nearly 500 days on the front line and relied on drones for supplies. The evacuation took 1 hour 14 minutes over 39 miles (62 kilometers), with the drone carrying up to 200 pounds (90 kilograms). Napalm, a programmer with the 92nd assault brigade, called the mission a historic step toward systematic aerial evacuations. The drone was equipped with carabiners and a winch to secure the injured soldier in a harness. Ukraine’s Army shared a video of the operation on October 19, marking a significant advancement in battlefield rescue capabilities.

item.title: Baseus’ New Security Camera Uses Spotlight to Track Intruders
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Original headline: Baseus’ New Security Camera Keeps Intruders in the Spotlight
Baseus’ PrimeSentinel U2 Pro security camera uses a spotlight to track intruders. The device features two cameras: a 3K-resolution fixed camera with 8x zoom and a bottom-mounted unit with a spotlight that pans and tilts. The spotlight casts a sharp rectangle on detected individuals, tracking them up to 8 meters away at speeds up to 16 feet per second. It can also follow vehicles moving at 19 mph. The AI-powered tracking uses passive infrared sensors but raises questions about on-device processing, internet dependency, data security, and data retention. The camera is battery-powered with a 3W solar panel, offering up to a day of use with 40 minutes of sunlight. It includes color night vision, a siren, two-way audio, and detects people, vehicles, and pets. It supports 512GB microSD storage without cloud subscriptions. The camera is IP65-rated and available for preorder at $280 on Amazon, shipping in early November.

item.title: Google Home Speakers Face Data Usage Spikes and Firmware Issues
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central, PCMag Original headline: Google Home Speaker Data Usage Spikes Prompt User Concerns
Google Home Speakers have experienced significant data usage spikes, with users reporting devices consuming up to 6TB of data in a month and 140GB in a single day. Reddit and social media accounts detail instances of excessive data downloads, including one speaker transferring 3.3TB over a month. Reports suggest the issue stems from failed firmware updates creating a loop where devices repeatedly download and fail to install updates. Google acknowledged the problem, stating a fix is being deployed. Users also noted latency issues with Gemini AI integration, with some devices experiencing up to 30-second response delays. A software update intended to improve performance instead caused further delays. Concerns persist over unexpected data usage, particularly for underused devices, highlighting ongoing reliability challenges for Google's smart home ecosystem.

item.title: U.S. bans federal agencies from using DeepSeek AI over security risks
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services from Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and remove existing systems using its technology due to national security risks. Concerns include potential access to U.S. government data by Chinese authorities under Chinese law. The order extends to third-party products built with DeepSeek technology, though exceptions can be requested. China criticized the move as politicizing technology, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning calling it an overreach. The U.S. has previously restricted DeepSeek in national security systems, and the latest order expands these limits to civilian agencies. China is reportedly considering export bans on 23 AI technologies, including advanced models. DeepSeek faces global scrutiny since its R1 model caused market volatility in January 2025. OpenAI and Anthropic allege DeepSeek used model distillation to extract data from U.S. systems, a claim the U.S. government has supported.

item.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Early Access Trick Revealed
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: Want to Play Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Before Everyone Else? This Trick Will Unlock it Early
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's multiplayer mode unlocks on October 23, 2026, with staggered regional releases. Preordered digital buyers gain early access to campaign and DMZ extraction mode. Xbox players can access the game 17 hours early by changing their Activision account location to New Zealand, adjusting time zone settings on their console. PlayStation users face a more complex process, requiring a separate account with a New Zealand IP via VPN and purchasing from the New Zealand store, which may involve currency conversion and is not guaranteed to work. Preorders are available on Xbox, PlayStation 4, Nintendo Switch 2, and PC platforms. Activision confirmed server demand will be high at launch, with peak beta player counts reaching 115,145 concurrent users.

item.title: Figma Co-Founder Criticizes MCP as Imperfect Protocol
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: Figma co-founder Dylan Field thinks MCP is not a perfect protocol
Figma co-founder Dylan Field acknowledged MCP's limitations while announcing expanded support for the open-source protocol. The company added 20 new MCP partners, including Amp, Notion, and Mistral. Field previously criticized MCP, noting Anthropic, the protocol's co-creator, does not expose resources via MCP. He tweeted, 'I find it interesting that Anthropic... do not expose artifacts/other cloud resources created via MCP.' Field later clarified Figma plans to support Pi. He stated MCP is 'not a perfect protocol' with 'tons of room for improvement' and favors frontier labs. Figma CEO explained the company avoids full openness to prevent data abuse, despite most users not intending malicious use. Field emphasized the need for a protocol users can 'use when they want to use their Figma data.'

item.title: Intel seeks FCC waiver to use foreign-made AGVs
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Intel asks FCC for waiver to buy foreign robots
Intel has requested the FCC to exempt its automated guided vehicles (AGVs) from a blanket ban on foreign-made robots. The company uses AGVs to transport sensitive materials in its chip manufacturing process, which are critical for maintaining cleanroom conditions. Intel argues that these AGVs fall under the FCC’s Covered List, which prohibits foreign-made robots, and that there are no domestic alternatives. Switching to local suppliers would require years of development, jeopardizing U.S. chip production. Major AGV suppliers include Japanese firms like Murata Machinery and Daifuku, with smaller South Korean and Taiwanese companies also in the market. Intel seeks a conditional waiver to continue using its AGVs, citing uncertainty over compliance with FCC rules. Other chipmakers, including TSMC, Samsung, and Elon Musk’s Terafab, may need similar exemptions as they expand U.S. manufacturing. The FCC’s policies aim to boost domestic production but have restricted companies like DJI and TP-Link from updating products unless made in the U.S.

item.title: ADHD Linked to 70% Higher Early Death Risk, Medication May Help
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Original headline: People With ADHD Face a 70% Higher Risk of Early Death. This Seems to Help
ADHD is linked to a 70% higher risk of early death from any cause, according to a meta-analysis of 19 studies involving over 15 million people. The research, published in JAMA Network Open, found ADHD was associated with a 90% higher suicide risk, 55% higher injury-related death rate, and 27% higher natural death rate. Medication use reduced early death risk by 25% among ADHD patients. Lead author Lucy Corrigan noted the findings suggest medication may support ADHD health but emphasized the need for more research due to study limitations. The analysis also highlighted ADHD’s potential to shorten lifespan, though the exact impact remains unclear. Researchers caution that ADHD diagnosis rates vary globally, with debates over overdiagnosis versus cultural factors. Proper treatment and support are recommended to mitigate health risks for ADHD individuals.

item.title: Russia's Satellite Approaches U.S. Commercial Satellite in Close Proximity
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Original headline: Russia Just Did Something Menacing in Orbit That Satellite Trackers Say Is a First
Russia's Cosmos 2612 satellite conducted close-proximity maneuvers near the U.S.-operated ICEYE-X36 commercial satellite between October 15 and 19, according to space-tracking data. The Russian satellite spent two days within less than 3 miles (5 kilometers) of ICEYE-X36 before moving to 62 miles (100 kilometers). Experts called the operation unprecedented in its proximity to a commercial satellite, with Jonathan McDowell noting it was the first low-Earth orbit rendezvous without the target satellite's owner's approval. The maneuvers, described as deliberate by LeoLabs and satellite-tracking specialist Marco Langbroek, raised concerns about potential anti-satellite weapon development. ICEYE-X36, operated by ICEYE US, provides synthetic aperture radar imagery to Ukraine. This follows previous Russian satellite activities targeting U.S. assets, but the recent incident highlights new risks to commercial space operations. Analysts warn that Russia's history of testing on-orbit weapons means the Cosmos 2612 could threaten Western satellites, aligning with broader aggressive gray zone activities against U.S. and European interests.

item.title: Pangram AI Detector Excels at Pure AI Detection, Struggles with Edited Text
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Original headline: Pangram review: A polished AI detector that gets the basics right
Pangram, a newer AI detection tool launched in 2023 by Brooklyn-based Pangram Labs, excels at identifying fully AI-generated text and human writing with high accuracy. It offers detailed classification results, a polished interface, and features like file uploads, OCR, and plagiarism checking. The free tier allows 2,000 words per day, while paid plans start at $20/month for individual use. Pangram claims to detect AI outputs from major models like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, with a reported 1 in 24,000 false-positive rate. Testing showed it reliably flags pure AI text and human writing but struggles with heavily edited AI content or mixed human-AI passages. It provides segment-level analysis, color-coding text by classification and confidence levels. However, it often misclassifies edited AI text as entirely human or AI-generated. The tool supports batch processing, Chrome/Firefox extensions, and integrations with education platforms. While effective for clear-cut cases, its reliability diminishes with complex, blended content.

item.title: Android Auto may support Work Accounts for drivers

Android Auto may soon support Work Accounts, allowing users to separate work and personal profiles. Tipster AssembleDebug discovered the feature in app code, suggesting a toggle in Quick Settings to enable work notifications on car displays and a briefcase icon. While not fully functional, the feature could support Google Meet and other Workspace apps. Recent updates include a redesigned Play Store with curated apps and YouTube switching to audio-only during driving. However, foldable phones like the Motorola Razr faced issues with missed notifications unless opened, prompting fixes from Motorola and Google. The Work Account feature aims to keep drivers engaged without distractions, though details remain speculative.

item.title: Hisense U6SF Pro: Affordable Mini-LED TV with Strong Features
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Original headline: Hisense U6SF Pro review: a richly hued mini-LED TV with strong features, especially for the price
The Hisense U6SF Pro is a 4K mini-LED TV with 144Hz refresh rate, HDR support, and built-in Alexa+. Priced at $650 for the 65-inch model, it offers features like Fire TV, WiFi 6, and a subwoofer. While it has good color coverage and decent audio, issues like vignetting and shadow detail limitations persist. The TV lacks hands-free Alexa control and a game-specific menu. It competes in the mid-range market, available in sizes from 55 to 100 inches. Sound quality is adequate for casual use but falls short of home theater standards. AI features like Hi-View Engine and Ambient mode are included, though the latter has limited practical value. The TV supports Dolby Vision IQ and DTS: Virtual X, with a 50-watt 2.1 speaker system.
