item.title: 16-Year-Old Router Flaw Remains Unfixed Despite Reports
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Original headline: Millions of routers have a 16-year-old flaw that nobody plans to fix
A 16-year-old security flaw called WPSplinter affects millions of routers from Asus, Netgear, Cisco, and other brands. The Broadcom software vulnerability allows remote code injection by bypassing security permissions through manipulated WPS codes. Despite being known since 2010, no full fix exists. Broadcom released a partial patch in 2018 but shifted responsibility to manufacturers, who failed to implement solutions. Security researcher Quentin Kaiser reported the flaw again in July 2026, but Broadcom cited its existing patch, which did not fully resolve the issue. Manufacturers also could not provide a fix. Disabling WPS does not fully mitigate the threat, leaving devices vulnerable. No complete list of affected models is available, complicating efforts to address the flaw. Users are advised to contact support for their specific router model and year of manufacture.

item.title: Critical Open-Source Software Relies on Underpaid Maintainers, Looming Risks
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Modern software is built on the backs of low-paid maintainers, opening the door to potential threats
Critical open-source software relies on underpaid or unpaid maintainers, raising security risks. A report highlights that 11 out of 23 essential projects have one or two maintainers, with scarce funding. Examples include Bash, maintained by Chet Ramey, and ImageMagick, managed by Dirk Lemstra. Log4Shell and libwebp vulnerabilities underscore the dangers of understaffed projects. SQLite, used in WhatsApp and Android, is maintained by four individuals who removed their names for safety. Curl, now funded by Open Collective and Germany's Sovereign Tech Agency, contrasts with projects like OpenSSL and Log4j, which also received agency support. The report argues that industry stakeholders should invest in these projects, given their widespread use and the growing threat of AI-driven vulnerability discoveries.

item.title: Study Replaces Prehistoric Origin of Malta's Cart Ruts with Classical Date
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Original headline: Archaeologists Thought Malta’s Mysterious Stone ‘Railways’ Were Prehistoric. The Evidence Tells a Different Story
Joel Grima, a PhD student at the University of Malta, challenges the long-held belief that Malta’s cart ruts date to prehistoric times. His study, published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports, argues that the tracks likely originated during the Classical period, spanning from the Phoenician colonization of Malta (700 BCE) to the end of the Byzantine period (870 CE). Grima’s analysis of stratigraphic and contextual evidence, along with digitized site models, supports this later dating. The cart ruts, found in dense networks across Malta, are compared to similar tracks in Europe, Asia, and North America, but their density and scale make them unique. While some ruts may predate the Classical period, the study emphasizes that a significant portion is securely dated to this era. Researchers remain divided on whether the grooves were intentionally carved or formed naturally by traffic. Despite unresolved questions, Grima’s work highlights progress in understanding the ruts through advanced analysis.

item.title: MIT engineers create recyclable thermoplastic yarn from polyethylene
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Original headline: Melt it, spin it, use it again
MIT engineers developed a thermoplastic yarn from polyethylene, a material found in milk jugs and grocery bags. This yarn can be melted and respun into new fibers without losing strength or flexibility, offering a solution to textile waste. Conventional elastic yarns require separating spandex from polyester or nylon for recycling, a process that is impractical. The MIT team created a stretchy yarn from two polyethylene variants, which can be knitted and woven into garments. Svetlana Boriskina, who led the research, said the material could be recycled indefinitely, supporting a circular textile economy. After 10 cycles of melting and respinning, the yarn retained its properties. The innovation aims to reduce landfill waste by enabling garments to be repurposed into new clothing without degradation.

item.title: The Prestige returns to theaters in IMAX and 70mm for 20th anniversary
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Original headline: ‘The Prestige’ Re-Release Is Coming to IMAX
Christopher Nolan’s The Prestige returns to theaters for its 20th anniversary, featuring IMAX and 70mm screenings. Nolan expressed excitement about audiences experiencing the film in these formats for the first time. The revival follows the success of other Nolan films like Interstellar and Tenet, which also returned to theaters in premium formats. Released in 2006 as an adaptation of Christopher Priest’s novel, the film stars Hugh Jackman and Christian Bale as rival magicians competing to perfect a teleportation illusion. It received critical acclaim and Oscar nominations for art direction and cinematography. The Prestige is noted for containing the first-ever IMAX 70mm shot used in a narrative-length film, a technique Nolan tested for The Dark Knight. The re-release, including the historic scene, opens in theaters on January 29, 2027.

item.title: Physician founded nonprofit to support brain injury patients
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Original headline: A champion for brain injury patients
Alissa Totman, a physician at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, specializes in treating brain injuries. She founded Synapse, a nonprofit supporting individuals with head trauma, stroke, and brain tumors, during her master’s degree at Harvard in 2016. The organization, originally started with Jaclyn Konopka during medical school, now has chapters at 28 universities. Totman emphasizes the need for more resources like Synapse. Her work began at MIT BrainTrust, where she connected with brain injury patients as a student. She continues leading Synapse while practicing medicine, highlighting the importance of peer support for patients. 'There’s a big need for more resources like this,' she says.

item.title: Anthropic proposes AI safety bill to block models with 50+ death risk
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
Anthropic has proposed a draft bill to Congress that would block AI models if their release poses a 'foreseeable, imminent risk' of over 50 deaths or a billion dollars in property damage. The scenarios include risks from biological weapons, model evasion of controls, or cyberattacks. The bill mirrors California’s SB53, which defines such risks as catastrophic. It suggests using independent evaluators registered with the U.S. Commerce Department to assess models, with payments allowed as long as they are not tied to evaluation outcomes. Evaluators would have 72 hours to report risks, after which the Commerce Department would seek a court order to halt distribution. Anthropic’s spokesperson confirmed the bill aligns with its Advanced AI Framework. While the proposed thresholds are theoretical, current industry concerns focus on agentic hacking incidents. Unlike Nvidia, which opposes new laws, Anthropic’s proposal advocates for a voluntary system of third-party evaluators to monitor AI models for risks.

item.title: YouTube might be testing hiding the dislike button
item.description:
Source: The Verge
YouTube appears to be testing the removal of the dislike button from video interfaces. Users on X and Reddit report the button is now hidden in the three-dots menu, making it harder to access compared to its previous placement next to the like button. One user noted the change would reduce its use. Google has not commented on the test, which follows past actions like hiding public dislike counts in 2021 and removing the dislike button from YouTube Shorts earlier this year. The test’s rollout scope remains unclear, with no indication of when or how widely it may be implemented.

item.title: iPhone Duo: Key Considerations Before Purchase
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: Five things you should know before buying the iPhone Duo
Pre-orders for the iPhone Duo begin Friday, with shipments starting October 23. Priced at $1,999, it's the most expensive iPhone yet but lacks features like a telephoto lens, variable aperture, and the Action Button. The Duo uses Touch ID instead of Face ID and has a lower-resolution front camera. Apps may not fully adapt to the foldable screen, with some appearing stretched or with black bars until developers update. Competitors include the Galaxy Z Fold 8 ($1,899) and Pixel 11 Pro Fold ($1,899), both with better cameras. Apple offers trade-in discounts up to $885 and installment plans. Accessories like the Duo Case ($79) and Duo Folio ($129) are available. The iPhone Duo is the first foldable iPhone but lacks Apple Pencil support until later this year. Reviews are pending, and Apple allows 14-day returns.

item.title: Acer Googlebook 14: Affordable 2-in-1 with OLED Screen and Design Flaws
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Original headline: Acer Googlebook 14 review
The Acer Googlebook 14 is the first 2-in-1 device in the Googlebook lineup, priced at $899/£999. It features an Intel Core Ultra 5 processor, 16GB RAM, 512GB storage, and a 14-inch OLED touchscreen with 2880 x 1800 resolution. The laptop’s magnesium-aluminum alloy chassis, fingerprint scanner, and thin design (2.51 lbs) position it as a premium alternative to the MacBook Air. It includes 12 months of Google AI Pro, YouTube Premium, and GeForce Now, plus a limited-time sustainability bundle with a 100W charger and tree-planting initiative. However, Googlebook OS feels underdeveloped compared to Windows 11, with limited app support and a disappointing battery life. The device offers three USB-C ports (one Thunderbolt 4) and an audio jack, but lacks traditional ports. While praised for its sleek design and responsive keyboard, the Acer Googlebook 14’s high price and OS limitations may deter some buyers, making it better suited for Android users seeking a MacBook-like experience.

item.title: Slate Opens Chicago Showroom for $25,000 Electric Truck
item.description:

Slate opened its first showroom in Chicago's Fulton Market District to showcase its $24,950 electric truck. The vehicle features manual windows, a minimalist interior, and a 205-mile range. The showroom, staffed by former Tesla employees, allows customers to view prototypes, customize options, and preorder the truck with a $300 deposit. Manager of Customer Experience Steve Purdy noted strong interest since the showroom opened on October 15, describing the response as 'incredible.' The space blends industrial and modern aesthetics, with visitors interacting with the truck and staff. The company aims to capitalize on the American pickup truck market with its bare-bones electric design.

item.title: Marvel Rivals Launches Avengers Endgame-Inspired PvE Event
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Original headline: The Next ‘Marvel Rivals’ Event Makes You Feel Like You’re in ‘Avengers: Endgame’
Marvel Rivals is launching a PvE event inspired by Avengers: Endgame as part of its 'Path to Doomsday' saga. The event, titled 'Avengers: Endgame: Encore,' features 50 players battling Thanos and his army at the Avengers Compound. The final victory triggers a snap that defeats Thanos, mirroring the film's climax. The event emphasizes nostalgia for the 2019 movie, with players experiencing the iconic Thanos defeat sequence. item.title: Samsung Introduces Rollable Phone Concept for 2027
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Original headline: Samsung Has Already Found the Next Way to Unfold a Phone
Samsung's 2027 foldable lineup includes a new rollable phone concept called the Galaxy Z Slide, according to a leak by tipster Anthony. The device features a horizontally expanding display, similar to prototype rollable TVs, and is part of a "4+4" strategy launching four conventional phones and four foldables in 2027. The Z Slide, first trademarked in 2021, builds on earlier concepts shown at CES 2025, which demonstrated slideable form factors expanding from 5.1 to 6.7 inches. South Korean outlet Money Today previously reported development of the Z Slide for 2028, but the leak suggests it could debut earlier. item.title: Windows 11 Bing Wallpaper App Redirects to Bing as Adware
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: Windows 11 Wallpaper App Is Acting Like Adware for Bing
The Windows 11 Bing Wallpaper app now redirects users to Bing.com when they click the desktop background, according to Windows Latest. Microsoft has been promoting Windows as a competitive OS against SteamOS, macOS, and Googlebooks, but the app's behavior has drawn criticism. Unlike past trials where users could disable the feature, the current version limits redirection to once every 24 hours. After redirecting, the app prompts users to set Bing as their default search engine and install a Wallpaper extension that adds daily wallpapers to new tabs. Enabling these actions automatically increases Edge browser usage. This adware-like behavior follows previous backlash over the app promoting a Harry Potter TV series. The app's intrusive tactics aim to boost Bing's visibility and user engagement.

item.title: Next Xbox could cost up to $1,800, report says
item.description:

The next Xbox, Project Helix, could cost up to $1,800, according to Fortune. The console, a handheld device slated for 2027 with a full version arriving in 2028, faces high production costs due to shortages and AI-driven component price spikes. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma described Project Helix as a 'family' of devices, including multiple releases. The projected price range of $1,200 to $1,800 may hinder Microsoft's goal of reaching 1 billion daily users, as current prices could deter buyers compared to cheaper alternatives like the Steam Machine. A potential Game Pass overhaul with la carte pricing for add-ons is also in the works. Additional Xbox layoffs are expected this month, with more cuts planned for November and January. The high price could challenge Xbox's growth from its current 100 million daily active users.

item.title: TP-Link seeks U.S. manufacturing alliance to bypass router sales ban
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: TP-Link proposes $1 billion US Wi-Fi router manufacturing alliance with Key Tronic
TP-Link, a U.S.-based company with Chinese roots, seeks to resume U.S. sales of Wi-Fi routers by forming a $1 billion manufacturing alliance with Key Tronic. The partnership aims to assemble routers in Corinth, Mississippi, to comply with U.S. government restrictions that banned foreign-made routers due to security concerns. The FCC added TP-Link to its Covered List in March 2026, citing risks from foreign-produced routers. State attorneys general from Florida, Montana, Iowa, and Nebraska sued TP-Link, alleging false claims about security and ties to China. TP-Link denies these allegations, calling them baseless and politically motivated. The company argues its U.S. market share of 65% is at risk due to the ban, which blocks its latest Wi-Fi 8 routers. To secure FCC approval, TP-Link emphasizes its 'America-first' strategy and claims the partnership will create jobs and support domestic manufacturing. The move comes as competitors like Amazon and Asus gained conditional FCC approvals, while TP-Link faces ongoing legal and regulatory hurdles.

item.title: Skylum Luminar Offers One-Time Buy but Lags on Advanced Features
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: Skylum Luminar Review: The Cure for Subscription Fatigue Falls Short on Power Features
Skylum Luminar offers a one-time purchase alternative to subscription-based photo editing software, providing core tools and AI features via an annual subscription. Luminar’s pricing includes three tiers: Desktop Only ($129), All Platforms ($159), and Max ($199), with optional AI subscriptions. New features like Auto Adjust, Bokeh AI, and Skin AI enhance editing, while Spaces and mobile syncing improve workflow. The app supports most cameras but excludes niche models. Its interface combines library and edit views, with nondestructive tools and presets. Despite improvements, Luminar still trails competitors in raw processing and advanced editing capabilities.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer features hovercraft racing without actual podracing, evoking nostalgia for the franchise's past. Developers tap into nostalgia for the original podracing games, which predate Disney's acquisition of Star Wars. The game's roguelike mode allows players to rebuild a podracer, culminating in a final race against the antagonist. Despite its focus on racing, the game's narrative centers on the sport's enduring appeal and the corruption of its competitive spirit.

item.title: WD Elements 6TB HDD is recommended for simple home backups
item.description:

The WD Elements 6TB desktop HDD is a plug-and-play backup drive now priced at $315 on Newegg. TSA bins may spread germs; experts advise keeping phones out. Travelers are urged to avoid placing phones in security bins due to hygiene risks. item.title: Amulya Vishwanath: Physical AI is in its LEGO era
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: Ex-Nvidia-turned-VC Amulya Vishwanath: ‘Physical AI is in its LEGO era’
Amulya Vishwanath, founder of Techable Ventures, compares the current state of physical AI to the LEGO era, emphasizing foundational development. She previously worked at Nvidia and other tech firms before launching her venture capital firm. Vishwanath notes that the industry is focused on building basic components like robotic hands and actuators, which will eventually form advanced systems. She draws parallels to past technological eras, stating innovation will scale as these elements mature. Talent remains critical, she argues, with her firm positioning itself as a bridge between founders and top engineers. Vishwanath highlights the challenge of retaining talent amid competition from giants like Anthropic and Nvidia, leveraging her industry network to support startups. She asserts that the current phase is a necessary precursor to broader advancements in physical AI.

item.title: User tests 6 USB accessories that work with Android phones
item.description:

A user tested six USB accessories with their Android phone and tablet, finding several functional. item.title: Company Develops Pollution-Free Rare Earth Extraction Method
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Original headline: A cleaner path to rare earth metals
Tomás Villalón Jr. cofounded Phoenix Tailings, a company developing a pollution-free method to extract rare earth metals from mining waste. The process, which uses an electrochemical technique, generates no toxins and is carbon-free when powered by renewables. Villalón, who studied materials science and engineering, was motivated by childhood memories of smog in Monterrey, Mexico, where his family originated. The company claims its approach addresses the issue of over several billion tons of mining waste produced annually. Phoenix Tailings' team includes Villalón, Michelle Chao, Nick Myers, and Anthony Balladon. The method aims to decarbonize rare earth extraction, a critical step in reducing environmental harm from metal manufacturing. The company's technology could mitigate pollution from the mining ecosystem while supporting sustainable metallurgy efforts.

item.title: Free mobile game uses player data to boost ad revenue
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Original headline: The dark side of 'free' mobile games — how developers reverse-engineer your patience to milk ad revenue
Free mobile game Block Blast by Hungry Games allegedly uses player data to manipulate ad revenue. Developer Ayoships reverse-engineered the app's code, revealing mechanisms that adjust difficulty based on smartphone models, geographical locations, and ad interaction history. These factors estimate users' purchasing power, influencing gameplay to maximize ad exposure. The game reportedly employs 'Boost then kill' tactics, making rounds easier before abruptly increasing difficulty to encourage ad watching. Players may also face secret score boosts, making ad rewards appear more valuable. Code references like 'reward' and 'moreCleanSuccessRound' suggest designed confidence-building phases. These techniques blur the line between genuine achievement and algorithmic influence, raising ethical concerns about exploiting player frustration for revenue. Ayoships, an AI developer, warns of potential deliberate manipulation, though independent verification is needed. The findings do not confirm how frequently these adjustments occur or if all players experience them equally. Free access to Block Blast, which earned $127 million in ads from January to May 2026, highlights broader issues about ad-supported games monetizing user attention.
item.source: Latest from TechRadar US in News

item.title: Homeowner Adds Ethernet to Every Room for Under $50 Using Switch and Cables
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Original headline: How I added Ethernet to every room of my home for under $50
A homeowner achieved Ethernet connectivity in every room without major renovations by using an unmanaged Ethernet switch and running cables along baseboards. The setup cost under $50, with the core component being a Netgear 8-port switch priced around $18. By connecting the switch to the router and distributing ports to multiple devices, the homeowner secured stable connections for essential tasks. Cables were routed through walls and secured with adhesive clips to avoid visible wiring. While all devices share the same uplink to the router, the trade-off provided reliable performance over Wi-Fi. The solution avoided drilling and wall jacks, relying on long Ethernet cables and additional switches for multiple rooms. The homeowner emphasized stability over speed, achieving consistent connectivity without a full network overhaul.

item.title: TikTok Employees Warned of Child Safety Risks, Executives Did Not Act
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: TikTok staff raised child safety concerns, but executives reportedly failed to act
TikTok employees raised concerns about child safety risks, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide-related content, according to court records. Depositions from March 2026 reveal employees criticized executives for failing to address these issues, noting minors were appearing in purchasable sexual content and exploiting platform loopholes to access age-restricted material. The company also faces consolidated lawsuits with Meta, Google, and Snap, alleging addictive design targeting young users.

item.title: TA's encouragement led to student's academic success
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Original headline: A good TA: priceless
Leszek Pawlowicz, a teaching assistant at MIT in 1980, encouraged a student after they scored 49 on their first exam. He smiled and told them, 'I expect to see you double your score on the next quiz.' The student later achieved a perfect score on the next quiz and graduated with strong grades. Years later, the student reconnects with Pawlowicz, who sent a charming note. The student credits Pawlowicz's support for their academic success, highlighting the lasting impact of a supportive TA. The article also mentions other tech news, including AI developments and industry events, but focuses primarily on the personal story of mentorship and its influence on the student's academic journey.

item.title: Anker’s 10-in-1 Docking Station drops to $80 for first time
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Original headline: Anker’s new 10-in-1 laptop dock drops to $80 for the first time
Anker’s 10-in-1 Docking Station is now $79.99, its lowest price since September. The device includes HDMI, DisplayPort, USB-A, Ethernet, and SD/microSD slots via a built-in USB-C cable. It features a digital screen showing real-time data like port usage, wattage, transfer speeds, and temperature. A top button toggles the display, and a double-tap starts a 25-minute timer. MacBook users can only use dual monitors in mirrored mode. The dock requires a USB4 or Thunderbolt 3/4/5 port and does not include a charger. The 20% discount makes it a notable deal for compatible laptops.

item.title: Stop-Motion Film 'Wildwood' Debuts with Technical Marvels and Dark Themes
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Original headline: ‘Wildwood’ Will Take Your Breath Away
Stop-motion film 'Wildwood' debuts with technical marvels and dark themes. Directed by Laika co-founder Travis Knight, the film follows Prue McKeel, a teenager babysitting her brother Mac, after his kidnapping by a murder of crows. Prue and classmate Curtis journey into the magical Impassable Wilderness to rescue him, encountering a cast of anthropomorphic creatures. The story explores grief, parenthood, and magic, with a focus on the Dowager Governess' tragic backstory. While praised for its intricate stop-motion animation and layered performances, the film faces criticism for its sprawling plot and underdeveloped character arcs. The film includes violent scenes and a dark tone, contrasting with its visual splendor. Wildwood opens in theaters on October 23.
